item.mechanism: Sequential decomposition of hydride powders driven by formation enthalpy differences removes hydrogen and facilitates in-situ alloying, with Ta and Nb hydrides decomposing first, followed by Ti, Hf, and Zr hydrides.
item.system: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr blend of hydride powders (TiH2, ZrH2, HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5)
item.operating_conditions: Heating under vacuum from 100 to 1000 °C; dehydrogenation occurs between 300 and 750 °C
item.supporting_observation: In situ X-ray diffraction showed TaH0.5 and NbH start decomposing at ≈290 °C, while ZrH2 decomposes last at ≈720 °C, following the sequence of hydride formation enthalpy values.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism assumes the specific hydride blend; the text notes that the absence of α-Ti indicates Nb and Ta are already alloyed with nascent Ti, lowering the allotropic temperature.
quotes: The sequence of the hydrides decomposition closely follows the sequence of hydride formation enthalpy values for Ta (−34 kJ mol −1 ), Nb (−40 kJ mol −1 ), Hf (−64 kJ mol −1 ), Ti (−67 kJ mol −1 ), and Zr (−79 kJ mol −1 ).
First, TaH 0.5 and NbH start to decompose at ≈290 °C.
Subsequently, the Group IV hydrides decompose fully at i) ≈545 °C for TiH 2 and at ≈700 °C for β‐Ti (H‐rich), ii) at ≈460 °C for HfH 2 , and at ≈700 °C for HfH x , and iii) at ≈720 °C for ZrH 2 .

item.mechanism: Oxygen contamination during sintering stabilizes the α-HCP phase and raises the α-to-β transition temperature, preventing the formation of a single metastable β-BCC phase during slow cooling.
item.operating_conditions: Vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h followed by slow cooling (5 °C min −1 ); oxygen content measured at 0.996 wt.%
item.supporting_observation: The authors attribute the presence of α-HCP phase after slow cooling to dissolved oxygen, which increases the α-to-β transition temperature, requiring quenching from 1500 °C to obtain a single β-BCC phase.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism applies specifically to samples with high oxygen content (≈1 wt.%); the text notes that Jaroslav et al. found residual α-HCP even after quenching from 1200 °C due to oxygen.
item.alternatives_considered: Insufficient diffusion of elements during sintering was considered but ruled out because the α-HCP phase formed during slow cooling, not due to lack of homogenization.
quotes: They attribute it to dissolved oxygen accumulated during sintering, which increases the α‐to‐β transition temperature as oxygen is an α‐HCP stabilizer.
Based on the data shown in Figure 3a , we perform quenching from 1500 °C to ensure the α‐to‐β transition.
These results suggest that the α‐HCP phase and dual β‐BCC phases are formed during slow cooling after sintering and not by insufficient diffusion of each element during sintering.

item.mechanism: Interstitial solid-solution strengthening by oxygen and carbon significantly increases yield strength at high temperatures, outweighing the lack of Hall-Petch strengthening from coarse grains.
item.system: Sintered HfNbTaTiZr bulk samples with ≈1.0 wt.% O and ≈0.1 wt.% C
item.operating_conditions: Compression testing at 750 to 1100 °C; grain size ≈28 ± 14 µm
item.supporting_observation: The authors calculate that oxygen and carbon interstitials contribute 676 MPa and 95 MPa to yield strength respectively, explaining why sintered samples are stronger than arc-melted ones despite coarse grains.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism relies on the specific interstitial content (≈1 wt.% O); the text states Hall-Petch strengthening is not dominant due to the coarse grain size.
item.alternatives_considered: Hall-Petch strengthening was considered but dismissed because the microstructure has relatively coarse grains.
quotes: This indicates that oxygen interstitial strengthening may significantly increase yield strength in the current HfNbTaTiZr samples: using the above equations provides strengthening contributions of 676 and 95 MPa, respectively.
However, the microstructure here has relatively coarse grains (≈28 ± 14 µm), indicating that Hall‐Petch strengthening is not the dominant strengthening mechanism.
The sintered bulk samples show higher yield strength than arc‐melted samples, consistent with the interstitial strengthening of oxygen (≈1.0 wt.%), between 750 and 1100 °C.

item.mechanism: Silicide coating improves oxidation resistance by forming a protective layer where (Zr,Hf)O2 fills pre-existing cracks and Si diffuses inward, creating a self-healing mechanism that prevents spallation.
item.system: HfNbTaTiZr coated with silicide layers (MSi2 and MSi) via pack cementation
item.operating_conditions: Pack cementation at 950 °C for 24 h; oxidation testing at 1000 °C for 20 h under flowing air
item.supporting_observation: SEM and EDS showed pre-existing cracks filled with (Zr,Hf)O2 and a deeper incursion of the silicide layer, preventing run-away oxidation despite cracks in the brittle silicide layer.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is effective for the specific silicide coating formed; the text notes that cracks in the silicide layer are created during cooling due to thermal expansion mismatch.
quotes: Thus, Zr and Hf within the silicide coating react with oxygen to form the oxide, while Si is released and diffuses deeper in the specimen, increasing the depth of the coating.
Thus, the formation of (Zr,Hf)O 2 filling cracks and the growth of the silicide layer underneath it both prevent the run‐away oxidation of the surface via spalling.
This self‐healing mechanism ensures good oxygen resistance even with the existence of cracks in the brittle silicide layer.

item.mechanism: Low thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr is caused by lattice distortion and defects (grain boundaries, dislocations) which depress electron/phonon propagation, making it suitable for thermal insulation.
item.supporting_observation: The measured thermal conductivity (10–17 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) is lower than pure elements, attributed to the distorted lattice structure and defects similar to high-entropy Al0.3CoCrFeNi.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is attributed to the high-entropy nature of the alloy; the text notes that 3D printing porous architectures further improves insulation.
quotes: Low thermal conductivity has been reported in a high‐entropy Al 0.3 CoCrFeNi alloy, where the distorted lattice structure and many lattice defects (e.g., grain boundaries and dislocations) depress the electron/phonon propagation.

The thermal conductivity of sintered HfNbTaTiZr (Figure S1 , Supporting Information) is 10–17 (W (m K) −1 ) between 50 and 900 °C, which is lower than the thermal conductivity of pure Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr.
This low thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr makes it desirable for thermal insulation applications.

item.mechanism: Dehydrogenation of hydride powders removes surface oxide layers by releasing H2O (steam), facilitating sintering kinetics and densification.
item.system: Blend of TiH2, ZrH2, HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5 powders
item.operating_conditions: Heating under vacuum after hydrogenation; dehydrogenation between 300 and 750 °C
item.supporting_observation: The authors cite prior research suggesting atomic H reacts with O in oxides to form steam, removing the oxide layer and allowing better particle contact during sintering.
item.scope_limits: The text notes that reduction of TiO2 by H2 gas is thermodynamically unfavorable, but atomic H in hydrides makes the reaction favorable.
quotes: Though the reduction of TiO 2 by H 2 gas is thermodynamically unfavorable, prior researchers suggest that atomic H in hydride powder will have a negative free energy change after it reacts with O in TiO, TiO 2 , and Ti 2 O 3 to form steam.
The dehydrogenation mechanisms of a blend of TiH 2 ‐ZrH 2 ‐HfH 2 ‐NbH‐TaH 0.5 powder are first studied by in‐situ X‐ray diffraction.
The dehydrogenation process is reported to remove the oxide layer on the powder surface by releasing H 2 O (steam) which facilitates the subsequent sintering process.

item.mechanism: Dynamic recovery and recrystallization cause stress drops and softening in the flow stress during high-temperature compression, competing with the densification of porous lattices.
item.operating_conditions: Compression at 800, 900, and 1000 °C; strain rate 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹
item.supporting_observation: A decrease of stress after yielding was observed beginning at 900 °C, indicating dynamic recovery and recrystallization become dominant, while progressive densification leads to higher stress.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is temperature-dependent; at 800 °C, shearing behavior dominates, while at 900 °C and above, dynamic recovery/recrystallization and densification compete.
item.alternatives_considered: Cracks forming along shearing bands were observed and noted as a potential contributor to softening.
quotes: A decrease of stress after yielding is observed beginning at 900 °C, indicating that dynamic recovery and dynamic recrystallization may become dominant at this temperature, in comparison with the sample compressed at 800 °C.
After the initial stress drop, the progressive densification of lattices leads to higher stress and competes with the subsequent softening of the flow stress.
The stress drop after yielding at 1000 °C shown in Figure 4a may be due to dynamic recovery and recrystallization which were reported previously for arc melted HfNbTaTiZr.

item.mechanism: Substitutional solid-solution strengthening occurs when Hf and Zr diffuse into the β-BCC matrix during quenching, contributing to higher hardness due to their large atomic radius differences.
item.operating_conditions: Homogenization at 1500 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching
item.supporting_observation: The quenched sample shows higher hardness than the multiphase sintered sample, attributed to Hf and Zr diffusing into the matrix and causing substitutional solid-solution strengthening.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism applies specifically to the quenched state where Hf and Zr are dissolved in the β-BCC matrix; the sintered state has phase segregation.
item.alternatives_considered: Interstitial solid-solution strengthening from oxygen was also considered as a reason for higher hardness in the quenched sample.
quotes: After quenching, the metastable single β‐BCC sample shows a higher hardness than the multiphase, sintered sample, for two possible reasons: a) Hf and Zr diffused into the β‐BCC matrix and contribute to substitutional solid‐solution strengthening as Hf (0.225 nm) and Zr (0.160 nm) have the largest and smallest atomic radius within these five elements.
The hardness of the sample increases with sintering time mainly due to the densification of the alloy.

In addition, both the sample sintered at 1400 °C and the quenched sample show a higher hardness than the arc‐melted and hot isostatic pressed (HIP) sample, [ [42] ] which we expect to be due to the strong interstitial strengthening effect from oxygen and carbon.
